objective: The impact of compliance on AI business use and development: the EU AI Act, OECD standards, ISO AI standards, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and data sovereignty
secondaryObjectives: Principles and risks of responsible AI use: transparency, explainability, accountability, and risks such as bias introduction, accidental data leakage, IP exposure, overreliance, and hallucinations

The organization, the systems, the data and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You are the security and AI governance lead at Norrland Freight, a fictional logistics company hiring in the US and the EU. HR wants to use a vendor's AI model to rank applicants from next month. You chair three weekly reviews before go-live.
handover: The vendor hosts the model in the US and fine-tunes it on customers' data by default.
The company has no AI risk management process yet.
howItWorks: The board shows the risk register against the appetite, each stakeholder's support in words and the docket.
Move on a week at a time. A decision comes to you at each review; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Week 2: an EU applicant asks why they were rejected; no notice, log or human review exists, and a regulator complaint follows.
Week 3: an internal check finds the model ranks applicants with career gaps much lower, which hits women returning from leave; HR has already used it on a pilot.
Week 4: an applicant's subject-access request reveals their CV was used to train the vendor's model; the data protection authority opens an inquiry.

clsPrompt.title: How risky is this use?
clsPrompt.context: HR calls it 'just a productivity tool'.

choices.label: Classify it as high-risk employment use: require documented risk management, data governance, logging, applicant notices and human review of every rejection before go-live

effects.log: High-risk obligations are required before go-live.

choices.feedback: Recruitment and selection are high-risk uses under the EU AI Act; the obligations follow the use, not the vendor's label.

choices.label: Use it for US applicants only for now
choices.feedback: That avoids the EU rules for now but leaves bias and transparency risks unmanaged.

choices.label: Accept HR's view: it's a productivity tool
choices.feedback: Ranking applicants is high-risk employment use; skipping the obligations is non-compliant.

rmfPrompt.context: The company uses ISO 27001 for security; nothing covers AI.

choices.label: Adopt the NIST AI RMF (govern, map, measure, manage) alongside ISO/IEC 42001, and run it on the screener: bias testing on past applicants, documented limits, an owner

effects.log: The framework is adopted and applied to the screener.

choices.feedback: A recognized framework gives repeatable risk management; applying it finds the screener's bias before applicants do.

choices.label: Write a one-page checklist for this project
choices.feedback: Something, but not repeatable for the next AI system.

choices.label: Rely on the vendor's statement that the model is fair
choices.feedback: The deployer remains accountable; nobody tested the model on your applicants.

sovPrompt.title: EU applicant data in US training

choices.label: Use the vendor's EU hosting, opt out of training on company data in the contract, and add a data processing agreement

effects.log: EU hosting, no training on applicant data, a DPA signed.

choices.feedback: Data sovereignty and purpose limitation: applicant data stays where the law expects and isn't reused by the vendor.

choices.label: Strip names before sending data to the US region
choices.feedback: CVs stay identifiable without names, and the training default still applies.

choices.label: Accept the defaults to launch on time
choices.feedback: Applicant data goes abroad and into the vendor's training set without a legal basis.

scoring.modelReasoning: AI compliance follows the use: under the EU AI Act, recruitment and selection systems are high-risk and need risk management, data governance, logging, transparency and human oversight. A recognized framework such as the NIST AI RMF or ISO/IEC 42001 makes risk management repeatable, and the deployer stays accountable for testing the model on its own population. Data sovereignty and purpose limitation decide where data is hosted and whether a vendor may train on it.
